section.title: The Garden
section.sectionRationale: This is the second movement of the toledot of the heavens and the earth, which opens at 2:4. After the wide creation prologue, the author zooms in to ground level, retelling the making of the man and the woman within a garden God plants, and setting up the choice that chapter three will test.
section.thesis: The personal covenant God forms man from dust, breathes life into him, and settles him in a garden-home with work, a loving boundary, and a bride.
section.frameNote: Four scenes: the man formed from the ground; the garden and its rivers; the one command; and the making of a suitable helper.

verses.text: This is the account of the heavens and the earth when they were created, in the day that the {{yhwh|LORD}} God made them.
Now no shrub of the field had yet appeared on the earth, nor had any plant of the field sprouted, for the LORD God had not yet sent rain upon the earth, and there was no man to cultivate the ground.
But springs welled up from the earth and watered the whole surface of the ground.
Then the LORD God formed {{adam|man}} from the dust of the {{adamah|ground}} and breathed the breath of life into his nostrils, and the man became a {{nephesh|living being}}.

media.alt: The garden of Eden with a central tree and four rivers
media.caption: A garden God plants, watered by a river that branches into four.

verses.text: And the LORD God planted a garden in {{eden|Eden}}, in the east, where He placed the man He had formed.

Out of the ground the LORD God gave growth to every tree that is pleasing to the eye and good for food. And in the middle of the garden were the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.
Now a river flowed out of Eden to water the garden, and from there it branched into four headwaters:
The name of the first river is the Pishon; it winds through the whole land of Havilah, where there is gold.
And the gold of that land is pure, and bdellium and onyx are found there.
The name of the second river is the Gihon; it winds through the whole land of Cush.
The name of the third river is the Tigris; it runs along the east side of Assyria. And the fourth river is the Euphrates.
Then the LORD God took the man and placed him in the Garden of Eden to cultivate and keep it.
And the LORD God commanded him, “You may eat freely from every tree of the garden,
but you must not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; for in the day that you eat of it, you will surely die.”

media.caption: Two brought together as one flesh.

verses.text: The LORD God also said, “It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make for him a {{ezer|suitable helper}}.”

And out of the ground the LORD God formed every beast of the field and every bird of the air, and He brought them to the man to see what he would name each one. And whatever the man called each living creature, that was its name.
The man gave names to all the livestock, to the birds of the air, and to every beast of the field. But for Adam no suitable helper was found.
So the LORD God caused the man to fall into a deep sleep, and while he slept, He took one of the man’s ribs and closed up the area with flesh.
And from the rib that the LORD God had taken from the man, He made a woman and brought her to him.
And the man said: “This is now bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called ‘woman,’ for out of man she was taken.”
For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and they will become one flesh.
And the man and his wife were both naked, and they were not ashamed.

yhwh.gloss: LORD in small capitals stands for the covenant name of God, YHWH. From 2:4 the personal, covenant-keeping God draws near, not only Elohim the mighty Creator of chapter one.

adam.gloss: Man, and also the name Adam. It echoes adamah, ground, so the word itself says that man is taken from the earth he is made to tend.

adamah.gloss: Ground or soil. Man (adam) is formed from the ground (adamah); we are earthy creatures, given dignity only by the breath of God.

nephesh.gloss: A living being, a living soul. The breath of God makes the man a nephesh; life is a gift held from God, not a possession man owns.

eden.gloss: Delight or pleasure. Eden is a garden of God's own planting, the first place where God dwells with man, a pattern of the sanctuary to come.

ezer.gloss: Helper or ally. The same word is used of God Himself as Israel's helper, for example in Psalm 121; it speaks of strength brought alongside, never of inferiority.

basic.context: After the wide view of the seven days, Genesis zooms in. It retells the making of the man and the woman up close, in a garden God plants, so we see how personal the Creator is.
basic.hermeneutics: This is not a second, competing creation story; it is a close-up of day six. Some people read it as a contradiction, but as a zoom-in it fits chapter one. The command about the tree sets up the choice that comes in chapter three.
basic.originalLanguages: God's covenant name, the LORD, appears here. Man (adam) is drawn from the ground (adamah). And the woman is called a suitable helper (ezer), a strong word used even of God helping us, not a word for someone lesser.
basic.typology: The garden where God walks with people points forward to the temple and finally to the new creation. Adam, given work and a bride, points to Jesus, the true Man who wins a bride, the church.
basic.christ: Adam is a pattern of Christ. The deep sleep from which a bride is formed hints at Christ, from whose pierced side the church is born, and marriage itself pictures Christ and the church.
basic.god: God is personal and near: He forms, breathes, plants, commands, and provides. He is generous, you may eat freely; truthful, the warning is real; and kind, it is not good for the man to be alone.
basic.crossReferences: Ephesians 5 reads marriage as a picture of Christ and the church. Revelation 22 brings back the tree of life and the river. Jesus quotes this chapter on marriage in Matthew 19.
basic.oneStory: God settles His image-bearer in a garden-home with work, a boundary, and a bride. This is the good world that the next chapter will fracture, and that God will labour through the whole Bible to restore.

context.literary:
Genesis 2:4 opens with the formula 'This is the account,' the first of the toledot headings that divide Genesis into its movements. Each of them introduces what came out of the thing named, so 'the account of the heavens and the earth' tells what became of the world God made. The movement runs to the end of chapter 4, and Genesis 2:4-25 is its opening scene. The verse itself turns on a hinge: 'the heavens and the earth' becomes 'the earth and the heavens,' and the camera comes down from the sky to the ground.

The passage begins with a picture of lack, verses 5 and 6: no shrub, no plant, no rain, and 'no man to cultivate the ground.' Every lack is then met. God forms the man, plants the garden, waters it with a river and sets the man in it to work. A second lack follows in verse 18, 'It is not good for the man to be alone,' the first thing in the Bible called not good. The animals are formed and named, but 'no suitable helper was found,' verse 20, and the tension builds until God forms the woman and brings her to the man.

The scene climbs to the man's words in verse 23, the first recorded human speech in the Bible, set as poetry in balanced lines. The narrator then steps out of the story to comment, 'For this reason,' verse 24, applying the event to every marriage after it. Verse 25 closes the unit with nakedness and no shame, a line that sets up the next chapter both by what it says and by the wordplay that links it to the crafty serpent of Genesis 3:1.

The passage is also built for what comes next. The ground, the two trees, the one command and its warning, the man, the woman and their union are all placed carefully on the stage before chapter 3 tests each of them. Even the man's work frames the story: there is 'no man to cultivate the ground' in verse 5, and after the fall he is sent out 'to work the ground from which he had been taken,' Genesis 3:23.
context.historical:
For Israel the garden would have looked strikingly like a sanctuary. God 'walks' in it, Genesis 3:8, using the form of the verb He uses when He promises, 'I will walk among you and be your God,' Leviticus 26:12. Its entrance faces east, as the tabernacle's did. Gold and onyx, verse 12, were the materials of the priestly garments, and two onyx stones engraved with the tribes' names sat on the high priest's shoulders, Exodus 28:9. Cherubim guarded the garden after the fall, Genesis 3:24, as cherubim were carved into the walls of Solomon's temple among palm trees and open flowers, 1 Kings 6:29. The man is placed there 'to cultivate and keep' it, and the same pair of verbs describes the Levites' service of the tabernacle, Numbers 3:7-8. Israel's worship was, in part, a memory of Eden.

The geography is deliberately real and deliberately beyond reach. The Tigris and Euphrates were well known to every Israelite; the Pishon and Gihon are not identifiable with certainty. Havilah appears among the descendants of Cush in Genesis 10:7 and at the edge of the Ishmaelite lands, Genesis 25:18, and Cush was the land south of Egypt. Gihon was also the name of the spring in Jerusalem where Solomon was anointed king, 1 Kings 1:33. The river flowing out from Eden to water the world matched the ancient sense that the dwelling of a god was a place of abundant water, and later prophets use the same picture of the temple, Ezekiel 47:1 and 47:12.

Ancient Near Eastern texts also knew stories of humans made from clay. Genesis differs sharply. The man is not a servant made to spare the gods their labour; he is given a garden, good food and meaningful work, God's own breath and, finally, a companion God Himself brings to him. Israel also knew marriage within a world of arranged unions, polygamy and household economics. Genesis 2 sets against that world a pattern of one man and one woman, leaving and holding fast, as the design from the beginning, which is how Jesus reads it in Matthew 19:4-8.
context.canonical:
The garden becomes the Bible's picture of what was lost and what will be restored. Lot sees the Jordan plain 'well watered like the garden of the LORD,' Genesis 13:10. Isaiah promises that the LORD 'will make her wilderness like Eden and her desert like the garden of the LORD,' Isaiah 51:3, and Ezekiel 28:13-14 describes a figure 'in Eden, the garden of God,' adorned with gold and precious stones on God's holy mountain. Psalm 46:4 speaks of 'a river whose streams delight the city of God,' and Ezekiel 47 sees water flowing from the temple and trees along its banks whose leaves are for healing. Zechariah 14:8 sees 'living water' flowing out from Jerusalem.

The forming of man from dust shapes the Bible's language about human frailty and dependence. 'We are the clay, and You are the potter,' Isaiah 64:8. When God withdraws His breath, 'mankind would return to the dust,' Job 34:14-15, and at death 'the dust returns to the ground from which it came and the spirit returns to God who gave it,' Ecclesiastes 12:7.

The New Testament quotes this chapter repeatedly. Paul cites verse 7 when he contrasts 'the first man Adam' with 'the last Adam,' 1 Corinthians 15:45-47. Jesus quotes verse 24 as the Creator's own word on marriage, Matthew 19:4-6 and Mark 10:6-9. Paul cites it against sexual sin, 1 Corinthians 6:16, and calls it 'a profound mystery' about Christ and the church, Ephesians 5:31-32. He appeals to the order of the woman's making in 1 Corinthians 11:8-12 and 1 Timothy 2:13. And the last chapter of the Bible brings back the river and the tree of life, Revelation 22:1-2, now in a city where God and the Lamb dwell with their people.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to see that the God who made the heavens and the earth is the same LORD who had drawn near to them in covenant. Chapter 1 showed God's majesty; chapter 2 shows His nearness, and it deliberately uses His covenant name, the LORD, together with God. The Creator of the cosmos is not remote. He shapes the dust, plants a garden, speaks one clear word and brings a bride.

He also wanted them to understand what a human being is. The man is dust and breath at once, humble in origin and raised by God's own gift of life. He is given a place, a task and a word to live by. Life with God was never meant to be idle; it involves work, care for creation, obedience and love. The one command teaches that true freedom means living within the good limits of the One who gives everything else freely.

Finally, the chapter was written to shape Israel's homes. Marriage is not a human arrangement but God's design: He forms the woman, He brings her to the man, and His word establishes the pattern of leaving, holding fast and becoming one flesh. Israel's families were meant to reflect that original gift, even in a world where the pattern was often broken.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Most of the passage narrates what God did at the beginning and cannot be repeated: forming the man from dust, planting the garden, making the woman from the man's side. It describes a world before sin, so the details are not a manual for daily life; no one today is placed in Eden or given the command about the tree.

Some elements, however, are presented as patterns that carry forward. Verse 24 is marked as a general principle by the words 'For this reason,' and both Jesus and Paul treat it as binding: marriage is the union of a man and a woman, it involves a real leaving, a lasting holding fast and a one flesh union, and 'what God has joined together, let man not separate,' Mark 10:9. The call to work and care for the ground reflects a lasting human vocation. The pairing of generous permission with one limit models how God's commands work. What the passage does not prescribe is the precise shape of every marriage or family; those questions are taken up elsewhere in Scripture, always measured against this beginning.

debates.question: How does Genesis 2 relate to the account in Genesis 1?

views.label: Two separate sources
views.case: Many modern scholars see two originally independent accounts joined together, pointing to the different names for God, the different style and an apparent difference in order, since in chapter 2 the man seems to be formed before the plants and animals.

views.label: A focused retelling of day six
views.case: The traditional reading takes chapter 2 as a deliberate close-up. The 'shrub of the field' and 'plant of the field' of verse 5 are cultivated plants that need rain and a farmer, not the vegetation of day three. The forming of the animals in verse 19 can be read as the background to the naming, so some translations render it 'had formed.' The change of divine name fits the change of focus, from Creator of all to covenant LORD. Jesus quotes Genesis 1:27 and 2:24 together as one word from the Creator, Matthew 19:4-5.

debates.bearing: Whatever one concludes about how the book was composed, the text as it stands presents the two chapters as complementary, and the New Testament reads them together. The shift from the cosmic to the personal is itself the point.

debates.question: What is the knowledge of good and evil?

views.label: Moral autonomy
views.case: To eat is to claim the right to decide for oneself what is good and what is evil, apart from God's word. That fits the serpent's promise, 'you will be like God,' Genesis 3:5, and explains why the tree was forbidden rather than simply dangerous.

views.label: Mature discernment given too soon
views.case: Elsewhere knowing good and evil describes maturity or royal wisdom. Little children 'did not know good from evil,' Deuteronomy 1:39, and Solomon asks for a heart 'to discern between good and evil,' 1 Kings 3:9. On this view the knowledge was not evil in itself but was to be received from God in His time, not grasped.

views.label: Knowing evil by experience
views.case: Some take the phrase to mean learning evil from the inside, by doing it. The pair already knew good; by disobeying they came to know evil as well, and their first discovery was shame, Genesis 3:7.

debates.bearing: The views overlap. In every case the heart of the matter is trust: whether the man and woman will receive their understanding of good and evil from God's word, or seize it on their own terms.

debates.question: Does the woman's creation as 'helper' imply a difference in role?

views.label: Equal worth with an ordered relationship
views.case: Many read the order of creation, the man formed first and the woman made for him and from him, as the basis for a pattern of loving headship in marriage and the church. Paul appeals to it in 1 Corinthians 11:8-9 and 1 Timothy 2:13.

views.label: Equal worth without a built-in hierarchy
views.case: Others stress that ezer is most often used of God as Israel's help, Psalm 121:2, that 'suitable' means corresponding to him, and that rule over the woman appears only as a result of sin, Genesis 3:16. They read Paul's appeals in their particular settings, and note his own balance: 'woman is not independent of man, nor is man independent of woman,' 1 Corinthians 11:11.

debates.bearing: Both readings affirm what the text makes unmistakable: the woman is fully human, made from the same substance, a partner the man recognises as his own, and the answer to what was 'not good.' Neither view may use the passage to diminish her.

study.originalLanguages:
'Formed' in verse 7 is yatsar, the verb of the potter shaping clay. Its participle is the ordinary word for a potter, and Jeremiah watches one at work: 'so he formed it into another vessel,' Jeremiah 18:4. Isaiah draws the image out: 'we are the clay, and You are the potter,' Isaiah 64:8. The verb speaks of skill and intention, of hands on the material. The same verb is used for the animals in verse 19, but only the man receives God's breath.

That breath is neshamah, 'the breath of life,' nishmat chayyim. The word is used of God's gift of life in Job 33:4, 'the breath of the Almighty gives me life,' and of all who died in the flood, 'everything that had the breath of life in its nostrils,' Genesis 7:22. The man 'became a living being,' nephesh chayyah, the very phrase used for the 'living creatures' of Genesis 1:20 and 1:24. The man shares his creatureliness with the animals; what sets him apart is that God breathes into him personally. Paul cites the line in 1 Corinthians 15:45.

The man's task in verse 15 is 'to cultivate and keep' the garden, using abad and shamar. Abad means to work or serve, and is the ordinary verb for serving God in worship. Shamar means to guard, watch or keep, and is used for keeping God's commands. The two verbs appear together for the Levites, who 'perform duties' and attend 'to the service of the tabernacle,' Numbers 3:7-8. Adam's work is farming, but it is also priestly service in the place where God dwells.

'A suitable helper' in verse 18 renders ezer kenegdo. The second word combines a preposition, a word meaning 'in front of' or 'opposite,' and a pronoun. It describes a counterpart, one who stands face to face with the man as his match. The animals are paraded before him, verse 19, and none of them is kenegdo.

Verse 21 uses tsela for what God takes from the man, and the BSB footnote allows 'part of the man's side.' Elsewhere in the Pentateuch tsela is an architectural word, used of the 'side' of the ark, Exodus 25:12, and of the tabernacle, Exodus 26:20, and later of the side rooms of the temple, 1 Kings 6:5. The verb in verse 22 is literally 'built,' banah, rendered 'made' in the BSB: God builds the woman as a builder raises a house.

The man's poem in verse 23 turns on the pair ish and ishshah, 'man' and 'woman.' The sound match shows kinship, and 'bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh' is the language of family. Laban uses the same kind of expression to Jacob, rendered 'my own flesh and blood,' Genesis 29:14, and the tribes use it to David at Hebron, 2 Samuel 5:1. The 'deep sleep' of verse 21 is tardemah, the sleep that falls on Abram before God makes covenant with him, Genesis 15:12, and that fell on Saul's camp 'from the LORD,' 1 Samuel 26:12. God works while the man is passive.

Finally, 'be united' in verse 24 is dabaq, to cling or hold fast. Ruth 'clung' to Naomi, Ruth 1:14, and Israel is told, 'Hold fast to Him,' Deuteronomy 10:20. It is covenant language: marriage is a loyalty chosen and kept, not only a feeling.

typology.type: Eden as the first sanctuary, Genesis 2:8-15
typology.fulfillment: The garden has the marks of a temple: God walking in it, an eastern entrance, gold and onyx, a river of life and a man set to serve and guard it. The tabernacle and the temple, with their carved cherubim, palm trees and flowers, 1 Kings 6:29, were a return to Eden in miniature. Jesus speaks of 'the temple of His body,' John 2:21, the place where God and humanity now meet. In the end the whole city becomes a sanctuary garden with the river and the tree of life, Revelation 22:1-2. The type falls short because Eden could be lost and the temple destroyed; the final dwelling of God with His people is permanent, Revelation 21:3.

typology.type: The first man formed from dust and made a living being, Genesis 2:7
typology.fulfillment: Paul quotes this verse and draws out the contrast: 'The first man Adam became a living being; the last Adam a life-giving spirit,' 1 Corinthians 15:45. The first man was 'of the dust of the earth, the second man from heaven,' 1 Corinthians 15:47. Adam received life; Christ gives it. On the evening of His resurrection Jesus breathed on His disciples and said, 'Receive the Holy Spirit,' John 20:22, and the Septuagint uses the same verb for God breathing into Adam. The type falls short at the decisive point: Adam's life could be lost through sin, but the life Christ gives cannot die.

typology.type: The bride formed from the side of the sleeping man, Genesis 2:21-22
typology.fulfillment: While the man sleeps God opens his side and builds a bride, and brings her to him. Paul reads marriage as 'a profound mystery' about 'Christ and the church,' Ephesians 5:32, a husband loving his wife as Christ loves the church, His own body. Many early Christian writers saw a further echo at the cross, where a soldier 'pierced His side with a spear, and immediately blood and water flowed out,' John 19:34. John does not draw the link explicitly, so it is a reading rather than a stated type. But Christ does give His life for His bride, Ephesians 5:25, and she is presented to Him 'as a bride adorned for her husband,' Revelation 21:2.

typology.type: The river flowing out of Eden to water the earth, Genesis 2:10
typology.fulfillment: The river that watered the garden and branched out to the lands beyond becomes a prophetic picture of life flowing from God's presence: Ezekiel's river from the temple, Ezekiel 47:1, and the living water of Zechariah 14:8. Jesus stands up at the feast and says, 'If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink,' for streams of living water will flow from within those who believe, John 7:37-38. The river reaches its source in Revelation 22:1, flowing 'from the throne of God and of the Lamb.' The first river watered one garden; the last one heals the nations.

The tree of life stood in the middle of the garden as God's offer of life, and after the fall the way to it was guarded, Genesis 3:24. Christ promises that the one who overcomes will 'eat from the tree of life in the Paradise of God,' Revelation 2:7, and the last chapter of the Bible sets it on both sides of the river, yielding fruit each month, its leaves 'for the healing of the nations,' Revelation 22:2. Access comes through Him: 'Blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may have the right to the tree of life,' Revelation 22:14.

study.christ:
This chapter leads to Christ first through the figure of the first man. Paul quotes verse 7 and names Jesus 'the last Adam,' 1 Corinthians 15:45. The first Adam was formed from dust and received breath; the last Adam is 'from heaven' and becomes 'a life-giving spirit,' 1 Corinthians 15:47. Adam was placed in a garden to serve and guard it and was given a word to keep. He failed at every point. Christ comes as the obedient Man who serves His Father perfectly and guards those given to Him, 'I have not lost one of those You have given Me,' John 18:9.

The Gospel of John frames the passion with gardens. Jesus is arrested in a garden across the Kidron, John 18:1. He is buried in a garden where no one had yet been laid, John 19:41. On the first Easter morning Mary Magdalene thinks He is the gardener, John 20:15, and in a sense she is right. The One who rose is the true Adam, beginning a new creation in a garden. The same evening He breathes on His disciples and says, 'Receive the Holy Spirit,' John 20:22, echoing the moment God breathed life into the first man.

The chapter leads to Christ through marriage. Jesus quotes verse 24 as the Creator's word, and adds, 'what God has joined together, let man not separate,' Mark 10:9. He calls His hearers back to how it was 'from the beginning,' Matthew 19:8. Paul goes further and says the one flesh union of verse 24 was always pointing beyond itself: 'This mystery is profound, but I am speaking about Christ and the church,' Ephesians 5:32. Christ loves the church, gave Himself up for her, and nourishes and cherishes her as His own body, Ephesians 5:29. The man's joy in verse 23 is a faint echo of the joy of the Lamb at His wedding, Revelation 19:7.

It leads to Christ through the garden sanctuary. God dwelt with humanity in Eden, and the dwelling was lost. In Jesus, 'the Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14, and He speaks of His own body as the temple, John 2:21. The river and the tree of life return in the final chapter of the Bible, flowing from 'the throne of God and of the Lamb,' Revelation 22:1-2.

A caution keeps this honest. Not every detail of Genesis 2 is a coded picture of Christ. The four rivers, the gold and the animals are not allegories. The links above rest on the New Testament's own use of the chapter. What Genesis 2 gives is the pattern of true humanity, true worship and true marriage, and Christ is the one in whom each of them is fulfilled and restored.
study.god:
This chapter shows the same God as Genesis 1 from another side. There He speaks and worlds appear; here He stoops and works with His hands. He forms, breathes, plants, takes, places, commands, brings, closes and builds. The verbs show a God who is not only above His creation but personally involved in it. The covenant name, the LORD, joined to God, tells the reader that the Almighty Creator is the same God who later makes Himself known to Israel by name, Exodus 3:15.

He is the giver of life. The man is only shaped dust until God breathes into him. Life is never humanity's possession; it is always on loan. That is why Job can say that if God were to withdraw His Spirit and breath, 'all flesh would perish together,' Job 34:14-15, and why Paul tells the Athenians that God 'gives everyone life and breath and everything else,' Acts 17:25.

He is generous, and His generosity comes first. The command of verse 16 opens with permission, 'You may eat freely from every tree of the garden,' and only then sets a limit. The garden is full of trees 'pleasing to the eye and good for food,' verse 9. God's commands are not the grudging rules of a jealous master but the boundaries of a good home.

He is truthful. The warning of verse 17 is plain and serious: 'in the day that you eat of it, you will surely die.' God does not hide the consequences of disobedience. His word defines what is good and what is evil, and life depends on trusting it.

He is attentive and relational. 'It is not good for the man to be alone,' verse 18, is God Himself identifying a lack in His creation before the man does. The God who exists in fellowship made humanity for fellowship. He involves the man in the process, bringing the animals to him 'to see what he would name each one,' verse 19, and He honours the man's choices: 'whatever the man called each living creature, that was its name.'

He is the one who brings the bride. The woman is God's gift, and He Himself presents her to the man, verse 22, as a father might bring his daughter to her husband. Marriage is His idea and His work, which is why Malachi 2:14 can call the LORD 'a witness' between a man and 'the wife of your youth.'

And He is the true helper. The word ezer used for the woman is used most often of God, 'My help comes from the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth,' Psalm 121:2. The One who makes a helper for the man is Himself the helper of His people.

For worship, the chapter calls for humility and gratitude. We are dust that breathes because He breathed. Every good gift, food, work, beauty, marriage and friendship, comes from His hand, and even His limits are a form of His care.

crossReferences.note: Paul quotes Genesis 2:7, 'The first man Adam became a living being,' and sets beside it 'the last Adam a life-giving spirit.' The first man was of the dust of the earth, the second from heaven. Genesis 2 describes the beginning of the first humanity; Christ begins the second.

Jesus quotes Genesis 1:27 and 2:24 together as the Creator's word on marriage. He explains that divorce was permitted because of hardness of heart, 'but it was not this way from the beginning.' Genesis 2 is the standard to which Jesus calls marriage back.

Paul reads Genesis 2:24 as a profound mystery about Christ and the church. Husbands are to love their wives as their own bodies, as Christ nourishes and cherishes the church, His body. The one flesh union of the first marriage points to the union of Christ and His people.

The Levites are to perform duties and attend to the service of the tabernacle, the same two verbs used for Adam's task to cultivate and keep the garden in Genesis 2:15. The link shows Adam's work in Eden as a kind of priestly service in the place of God's presence.

Ezekiel speaks of Eden, the garden of God, adorned with precious stones and gold, including onyx, and set on the holy mountain of God with a guardian cherub. The picture confirms that Israel thought of Eden as a sanctuary, the mountain garden where God dwells.

In Ezekiel's vision water flows from the temple toward the east and becomes a river, with fruit trees on its banks whose leaves are for healing. It takes up the river of Genesis 2:10 and the trees of the garden as a picture of life flowing out from God's restored presence.

'My help comes from the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth.' The word for help here is ezer, the noun used for the woman in Genesis 2:18. The term used for the woman is the one Scripture uses most often of God's own help, which guards against reading 'helper' as a word for someone lesser.

If God were to withdraw His Spirit and breath, all flesh would perish together and mankind would return to the dust. Job draws out Genesis 2:7: human life exists moment by moment as the gift of God's breath, and without it we are only dust again.

On the evening of the resurrection Jesus breathed on His disciples and said, 'Receive the Holy Spirit.' As God breathed into the first man in the garden, the risen Christ breathes new life into His people, beginning a new creation.

Paul appeals to the woman's origin from the man and then balances it: in the Lord woman is not independent of man, nor man of woman, for as woman came from man, so man is born of woman, 'but everything comes from God.' He keeps Genesis 2 from being used to divide.

The LORD will comfort Zion and make her wilderness like Eden and her desert like the garden of the LORD, with joy and song. The prophets use the garden of Genesis 2 as the picture of the restoration God promises His people after judgment.

The river of the water of life flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb, and the tree of life stands on either side of it. The river and the tree of Genesis 2 return, now in a city, with healing for the nations.

study.oneStory:
Genesis 2 shows the good creation from the inside. Chapter 1 gave the world its shape; this chapter gives it a centre, a garden where the LORD God dwells with the man and woman He has made. It answers the question of what human life was designed to be: life with God, in a place He prepared, with work to do, a word to trust and a partner to love.

It also sets the stage for everything that follows. The tree of the knowledge of good and evil, the command, the warning of death, the man formed from the ground and the woman formed from the man are all placed carefully in the story so that chapter 3 can test them. When the test fails, each gift is damaged. The ground is cursed, the work becomes toil, the marriage is strained, shame replaces nakedness without shame, and the way to the tree of life is barred. The man who was formed from dust is told he will return to it, Genesis 3:19.

The rest of the Old Testament keeps the memory of the garden alive. The tabernacle and temple are built with garden imagery, and priests serve and guard them as Adam was meant to serve and guard Eden. The promised land is described as a place of abundance, and the prophets promise that the wilderness will become like Eden, Isaiah 51:3. Marriage, with all its failures, remains a sign of the original design, and the prophets use it to picture God's covenant love for Israel.

In Christ the garden story begins again. He is the last Adam who obeys where the first failed. He is arrested in a garden, buried in a garden, and rises in a garden, and He breathes new life into His people. He is the Bridegroom who gives Himself for His bride, and He is the true temple where God dwells with humanity.

The Bible ends with Eden restored and surpassed. The river of the water of life flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb, and the tree of life stands on either side of it, Revelation 22:1-2. The bride is ready for the marriage of the Lamb, Revelation 19:7, and the dwelling place of God is with man, Revelation 21:3. The garden has become a city, but it is still a home where God and His people live together, and His servants worship Him there, Revelation 22:3.

sermon.title: The First Wedding Day (Genesis 2:18 to 25)
sermon.why: Keller shows how the first marriage in Genesis 2 opens the whole storyline of the Bible, which ends with the wedding of the Lamb, and draws out marriage as a picture of the gospel. A clear, orthodox treatment of this passage.

quiz.q: Why does Genesis 2 tell the making of man again after chapter 1?

options.text: It is a close-up of day six, zooming in on the man, the garden, and the woman.
options.note: Chapter 2 is a topical zoom on day six, not a rival account.

options.text: To add details like the garden and the naming of the animals.
options.note: True detail, but it misses that the chapter is a zoom-in on day six.

options.text: Because it is a separate, later creation by a different author.
options.note: This overreads source theories against the unity of the text.

options.text: Because chapter 1 was a mistake being corrected.
options.note: The chapters complement; they do not correct one another.

quiz.q: What does the word for suitable helper, ezer, tell us about the woman?

options.text: She is a strong helper brought alongside; the same word is used of God helping His people.
options.note: Ezer implies strength and alliance, used even of God, never inferiority.

options.text: She is a companion so that the man is not alone.
options.note: True, but it misses the strength the word carries.

options.text: She is an assistant of lesser standing.
options.note: The word does not imply lesser worth; it is used of God Himself.

options.text: She is an afterthought outside God's plan.
options.note: God deliberately says it is not good for man to be alone and provides her.

quiz.q: What is the significance of the one command about the tree?

options.text: It is a real boundary of loving command that leaves room for trust and obedience.
options.note: The single prohibition amid total generosity makes love and trust possible.

options.text: It is a test of whether the man will obey God.
options.note: True, but framed only as a test it can miss God's surrounding generosity.

options.text: It shows God did not want humans to have any knowledge.
options.note: God gives freely from every other tree; the issue is trust, not knowledge itself.

options.text: It was a trap set so the man would fail.
options.note: God warns truthfully and provides abundantly; it is not a trap.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament read Adam and the garden?

options.text: Adam is a type of Christ, and marriage pictures Christ and the church.
options.note: Romans 5 and Ephesians 5 read Adam and marriage as pointing to Christ.

options.text: As history that Jesus refers to.
options.note: True, Matthew 19, but it stops short of the typology to Christ.

options.text: As a nice story with no link to Jesus.
options.note: The New Testament explicitly ties it to Christ.

options.text: As unrelated to the gospel.
options.note: Paul makes it central to the gospel of the last Adam.

quiz.q: What is the main point of Genesis 2:4 to 25?

options.text: The personal covenant God forms man for communion with Him, for work, and for marriage within His good boundary.
options.note: This is the heart of the passage.

options.text: God made a garden and the first couple.
options.note: True, but it describes the events rather than the point about God and communion.

options.text: The passage is mainly about the geography of four rivers.
options.note: The rivers are detail, not the main point.

options.text: Humans are self-made and autonomous.
options.note: The passage shows man formed, placed, and provided for by God.

questions: You were formed from dust and given life by God's breath. How does remembering that you are both earthy and God-breathed change how you see your worth today?
God gave the man real work in the garden before the fall. How can you receive your daily work this week as a gift and a calling rather than only a burden?
God set one loving boundary in a garden of freedom. Where is God's 'you may not' actually an expression of His care, and are you trusting it?
God said it is not good for the man to be alone. Who has God given you for companionship, and how might you be a strong helper to someone this week?
Marriage here points to Christ and the church. Whether married or single, how does belonging to Christ as His beloved shape your identity?

translationNotes.note: LORD in small capitals renders the covenant name YHWH, distinct from the general word God, Elohim, used in chapter one. The pairing the LORD God binds the two together.
Suitable helper renders ezer kenegdo, a helper corresponding to him. Because ezer is used of God as Israel's helper, it carries no sense of inferiority.
